headline: CISA flagged a self-spreading npm attack that tried to steal credentials.
discoveryQuestion: Who on your team installs npm packages? And how are your dev and CI tokens scoped and rotated?
avoid: Do not name affected packages or suggest the account was compromised. Package-level impact is not verified here.

headline: CISA reported attackers actively exploiting affected versions of SolarWinds Orion.
discoveryQuestion: How does your team decide which vendor updates to trust? Who owns that check?
avoid: Do not claim any product would have prevented it. The victim list and attack techniques are outside this record's verified scope.

headline: Codecov said an attacker changed its Bash Uploader to pull data out of customers' CI environments.
discoveryQuestion: What third-party scripts run in your CI today, and which secrets can they see?
avoid: Don't say which customers lost secrets; that is not established.

headline: A popular GitHub Action had its version tags pointed at a malicious commit that printed CI secrets into workflow logs.
discoveryQuestion: Are your third-party Actions pinned to a commit SHA, or to tags that can move?
avoid: The 23,000 figure is repositories using the Action, not confirmed leaks.

headline: Malicious Nx packages stole developer tokens and SSH keys, then used installed AI coding CLIs to hunt for more secrets.
discoveryQuestion: Which AI coding tools run on your developers' machines? What can they read?
avoid: Don't present the initial token-theft route as confirmed.

headline: Malware on one engineer's laptop stole a 2FA-backed SSO session. CircleCI told every customer to rotate their stored secrets.
discoveryQuestion: If your CI vendor asked you to rotate every stored secret today, how long would it take?
avoid: Don't claim specific customer impact; the source covers the rotation advice, not individual customers.

headline: After the Okta breach, Cloudflare missed rotating one service token and three service accounts. An attacker used them to get into Confluence and Jira.
discoveryQuestion: After a vendor breach, how do you find every credential that needs rotating, even the ones you think are unused?
avoid: Don't name an actor; attribution is Cloudflare's own assessment.

headline: Per the FTC, intruders used reused passwords to get into a private GitHub repo, found an AWS key and reached Uber's S3 data.
discoveryQuestion: Do you scan private repos for cloud keys? Is MFA required on your code host?
avoid: This happened in 2016; don't present it as recent.

headline: Microsoft reported an attacker used an acquired consumer signing key to forge tokens and get into Outlook Web Access and Outlook.com.
discoveryQuestion: Where do your signing keys live? How would you know if key material left that environment?
avoid: Don't state how the key was stolen; Microsoft has not confirmed it.

headline: An admin GitHub token for Python's core organizations was sitting in a compiled .pyc file inside a public Docker image.
discoveryQuestion: Do your secret scans cover build artifacts and container images, or just source code?
avoid: PyPI found no malicious use; don't describe it as an attack.

headline: One over-scoped Azure SAS token in a public GitHub repo exposed 38TB of private Microsoft research data.
discoveryQuestion: How do you keep track of the scope and expiry of shared-access tokens your teams create?
avoid: Wiz reported no attacker activity; describe it as an exposure, not an attack.

headline: Attackers pulled AWS keys from exposed .env files at scale, targeting 110,000 domains.
discoveryQuestion: Could one of your web apps expose its .env file? Would you notice if those keys got used?
avoid: Don't name an actor or a number of extorted organizations; neither is stated.

headline: Okta said an attacker used a support-system service account whose password had been saved to an employee's personal Google account. They read support files from 134 customers and hijacked sessions at 5 of them.
discoveryQuestion: When your teams send HAR files or logs to a vendor's support, are session tokens stripped first? Who checks?
avoid: Don't name a customer beyond those Okta itself named, and don't present the personal-account exposure path as confirmed.

headline: Toyota said a contractor left a data server access key in public GitHub code for almost five years, putting up to 296,019 customer records at risk.
discoveryQuestion: Do your contractors' repos fall under your secret scanning, or only your own?
avoid: Toyota could not confirm the key was used; don't describe it as a confirmed theft.

headline: An attacker used a contractor's bought password and kept sending MFA push requests until one got approved. From there they moved into Slack and G-Suite.
discoveryQuestion: Do your contractors use push-approval MFA? Would you notice a burst of denied prompts?
avoid: Don't repeat the hard-coded PAM credential story; Uber's statement doesn't support it.

headline: Unit 42 reported attackers running an open-source AI pentest framework on commercial AI models. They carried out 25 operations and broke into 10 organizations.
discoveryQuestion: If an automated agent scanned you today, what would it find first? Sprayable logins, exposed APIs, old CVEs?
avoid: Don't name victims or state attribution as fact; Unit 42's assessment is moderate confidence.

headline: West Pharmaceutical's SEC filing reported data theft and encrypted systems that disrupted its operations worldwide.
discoveryQuestion: If key systems were encrypted tomorrow, which operations would stop? How fast could you restore them?
avoid: Don't name a ransomware group or give impact figures; the filing names neither.
